opus-5.5.text:
I think social media is the closest thing we have to a dress rehearsal, and honestly, we didn't do very well in it. So the first lesson is humility about our ability to see harms coming.

When social media arrived, the dominant story was connection: everyone gets a voice, information flows freely, communities form across distances. Much of that was true. But the society-level harms didn't show up as dramatic single events. They accumulated quietly, through incentives. Engagement-optimized feeds didn't set out to polarize people or damage teenagers' mental health. Those were emergent effects of systems built to capture attention at scale. By the time researchers had solid evidence, the platforms were embedded in politics, commerce, and people's daily lives, and the business models were locked in.

So when I look at AI, I ask a few questions shaped by that history.

First, what is the system actually being optimized for, and who benefits? With social media it was attention and ad revenue. With AI it might be engagement again, think of companion apps and chatbots designed to keep you talking, or it might be labor substitution or speed to market. The incentive tells you a lot about where the harms will come from.

Second, we have to look beyond individual interactions to aggregate effects. One person getting a slightly sycophantic answer from a chatbot isn't a crisis. Hundreds of millions of people outsourcing judgment, relationships, or their sense of what's true to systems tuned in particular ways could reshape society in ways no single conversation reveals. Social media taught us that the unit of harm is often the population, not the person.

Third, timing matters enormously. With social media we waited for proof, and the proof arrived after the window for easy intervention had closed. There's a real tension here. You don't want to regulate on speculation. But you also can't wait for a decade of longitudinal studies while the technology is deployed to billions. That argues for things like independent researcher access to data, transparency requirements, and monitoring built in from the start rather than bolted on after a scandal.

And finally, we shouldn't assume the harms will look the same. Some will rhyme with social media: manipulation, isolation, erosion of shared reality. Others will be genuinely new, because these systems don't just distribute content, they generate it and act on our behalf. The history should make us vigilant, not complacent in thinking we already know the playbook.

If there's one sentence I'd want people to take away, it's this: the time to shape a technology's incentives is before they harden into its business model. We missed that moment with social media. With AI, we're still in it, but barely.

r001.rationale: It says social media harms accumulated quietly and were recognized after platforms became embedded, then warns AI may produce genuinely new harms and urges vigilance. This frames AI risks as including harms we cannot yet anticipate.

r002.rationale: It discusses population-level effects and recommends researcher access, transparency, and monitoring, but does not ask how society-level harms from widespread AI use can be measured.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the social media story is the single most useful case study we have, mostly because we got it wrong in a very specific, repeatable way, and we can see the mechanics of how we got it wrong.

If you go back to the early 2010s, the debate about social media was almost entirely about individual harms. Is this app addictive? Is it bad for teenagers' sleep? Is screen time hurting attention spans? All of those questions were legitimate, but they framed the problem as something happening between one person and one device. And that framing is comfortable for companies, because it points to individual responsibility. Use the screen time tools. Set your own limits.

What we missed, or caught far too late, were the structural harms. The way engagement-optimized ranking reshaped the economics of journalism. The way it changed what kinds of political speech get amplified. The way it eroded shared facts, and made coordinated manipulation cheap. Those weren't anyone's individual experience. You couldn't see them in a single user's feed. They were emergent properties of billions of feeds interacting with each other, and with institutions that had no idea they were being reshaped.

So the first lesson for AI is: the harms that matter most at the society level are usually the ones that are hardest to see from the perspective of any single user. If you survey people about whether a chatbot was helpful to them today, you'll get overwhelmingly positive answers, and that will be true even if the aggregate effect is hollowing out some capability we depend on collectively. We should be deeply suspicious of individual satisfaction as the measure of success.

The second lesson is about incentives. Social media wasn't harmful because the people building it were malicious. It was harmful because the business model rewarded attention, and attention is captured most reliably by outrage and novelty. With AI, I'd ask: what is the equivalent metric? If it's engagement again, if it's time spent with a companion, if it's dependence, then we already know how that movie ends. If it's something more like trust or reliance on the model's judgment, that's a new kind of lever, and I'd argue a more consequential one.

Third, speed. Social media took about a decade to go from novelty to the primary information infrastructure for a large part of the planet. By the time serious researchers had data access and regulators had vocabulary, the structures were locked in. AI is moving faster, and the companies are more concentrated. So the window for shaping norms is shorter, not longer.

The last thing I'd say is that we should resist the temptation to just map the old harms onto the new technology. Misinformation, polarization, yes, those carry over. But the distinctly new risks are around things like the concentration of persuasive capability, the automation of relationships, labor displacement at a scale and pace we haven't managed before. The history of social media should make us humble about our ability to predict the specific harm, while making us much more confident that the harm will come from the business model and the deployment pattern, not from any single bad actor.

r001.rationale: The response says social media’s structural harms were missed or recognized too late, then applies that lesson to AI: society-level harms may be invisible to individual users, and we should be humble about predicting their specific forms. This communicates the risk of unanticipated harms.

r002.rationale: The response warns that individual satisfaction is a poor measure of success, but it does not ask how to measure society-level harms from widespread AI use.

astra-6.text:
I think social media should make us much more humble about our ability to anticipate what happens when a technology reaches billions of people. We focused on what these platforms let individuals do—connect, share, find information—and paid much less attention to how they would change the environment everyone lives in: the incentives for public discourse, the distribution of attention, our ability to agree on what’s true.

With AI, we need to ask those broader questions from the beginning. It’s not just, “Can this model give a harmful answer?” It’s, “What happens when millions of people, companies, and institutions use these systems, and their behavior changes in response?” A system can be useful in each individual interaction and still produce damaging collective outcomes.

And we should look at the business incentives. If companies are rewarded for capturing attention, encouraging dependence, or deploying faster than their competitors, good intentions won’t be enough. The lesson from social media is to make independent scrutiny and public accountability part of deployment, rather than waiting until the harms are widespread and the technology is difficult to change.

r001.rationale: It says social media should make us humble about predicting what happens at scale, then applies that lesson to AI’s broad societal effects. This conveys that AI risks may include outcomes we cannot anticipate in advance.

r002.rationale: It calls for independent scrutiny and public accountability, but does not ask how to measure harms from widespread AI use.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the history of social media should make us much more attentive to the gap between what a technology can do for an individual and what happens when it’s deployed across a society. You can have a product that people find useful, that they choose to use, and still create collective outcomes that nobody would have chosen.

With social media, we focused a lot on connecting people and giving everyone a voice. We were slower to ask what happens when the systems distributing those voices are optimized for engagement. How does that change what gets rewarded, who gains influence, or our ability to agree on what’s true? Those effects aren’t captured by asking whether a particular post is harmful.

We need to bring that same lens to AI earlier. Testing whether a model gives a dangerous answer matters, but it doesn’t tell us what happens when millions of people rely on it for information, companionship, or decisions. Nor does it tell us how institutions respond when producing persuasive content becomes incredibly cheap.

The lesson isn’t that AI will follow exactly the same path. It’s that we should examine incentives, business models, and feedback loops alongside capabilities. And we should build the ability to study and change these systems before society becomes dependent on them. With social media, we spent years treating the societal consequences as someone else’s problem. We have an opportunity to avoid repeating that.

r001.rationale: It describes social media’s collective effects as outcomes people did not anticipate or choose, then uses that experience to urge examining AI’s broader societal effects earlier.

r002.rationale: It says individual post or model testing does not capture societal effects, but does not ask how harms from widespread AI use can be measured.
